summary.text: The dot product takes two equal-length lists of numbers, usually coordinate vectors, and returns a single number.
Algebraically it is the sum of the products of matching entries; geometrically it is 𝐚⋅𝐛 = ‖𝐚‖‖𝐛‖cos θ, with θ the angle between them.
Two non-zero vectors are orthogonal exactly when 𝐚⋅𝐛 = 0, and a vector's length is ‖𝐚‖ = √𝐚⋅𝐚.

facts.label: Other names
facts.value: Also called the scalar product, and a kind of inner product

facts.label: Why scalar
facts.value: Its result is a scalar, not a vector

facts.label: Self dot product
facts.value: 𝐚⋅𝐚 is never negative, and is zero only if 𝐚 = 𝟎

facts.label: Orthogonality test
facts.value: 𝐚⋅𝐛 = 0 means orthogonal, for non-zero vectors

facts.label: No cancellation
facts.value: 𝐚⋅𝐛 = 𝐚⋅𝐜 does not force 𝐛 = 𝐜

options.label: Exactly one
The product of their lengths
The sum of their lengths

items.explain: Two non-zero vectors are orthogonal if and only if 𝐚⋅𝐛 = 0.

items.prompt: Why is the dot product also called the scalar product?

options.label: Its result is a single number, not a vector
It only works on lists with one entry
It first scales each vector down to length one
It multiplies each vector by a scalar first

items.explain: The name scalar product emphasizes that the result is a scalar rather than a vector.

items.prompt: You know a vector's dot product with itself. How do you get the vector's length?

options.label: Double it
Divide it by the angle
Take its square root
Subtract one from it

items.explain: The length of a vector is the square root of the dot product of the vector by itself: ‖𝐚‖ = √𝐚⋅𝐚.

items.prompt: With ordinary numbers, if ab = ac and a is not zero, then b must equal c. Does the same hold for dot products?

options.label: Yes, cancellation works for every pair of vectors
No, b and c can differ when their difference is perpendicular to a
Yes, but only in three dimensions
No, because the dot product is not distributive

items.explain: The dot product does not obey the cancellation law: 𝐚⋅𝐛 = 𝐚⋅𝐜 only means 𝐚 is perpendicular to (𝐛 − 𝐜), which can be non-zero.

items.prompt: You know two vectors' lengths and their dot product. What can you work out about their directions?

options.label: Which one is longer
Nothing, since direction needs the cross product
The cosine of the angle between them
Whether either one is a scalar

items.explain: Since 𝐚⋅𝐛 = ‖𝐚‖‖𝐛‖cos θ, the cosine of the angle is the dot product divided by the product of the lengths.

paragraphs.heading: Two lists in, one number out
paragraphs.text: The dot product takes two lists of numbers of the same length, usually the coordinates of two vectors, and gives back one number. It is also called the scalar product, a name that stresses the answer is a plain number, called a scalar, rather than a vector. The name dot product comes from the dot symbol, as in 𝐚⋅𝐛. Because it is a special case of an inner product, that term is often used for it as well.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to compute it
paragraphs.text: There are two ways to define it. The algebraic way: multiply the matching entries of the two lists, then add up those products. The geometric way: multiply the two lengths, then multiply by the cosine of the angle between the vectors, written 𝐚⋅𝐛 = ‖𝐚‖‖𝐛‖cos θ. When you work in Cartesian coordinates, the two recipes always agree.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring length and angle
paragraphs.text: In modern geometry, where space is often built from vectors, the dot product is what defines lengths and angles. Dot a vector with itself and you get the square of its length, so the length is ‖𝐚‖ = √𝐚⋅𝐚. Divide the dot product of two vectors by the product of their lengths and you get the cosine of the angle between them. So a single operation hands you both measurements.

paragraphs.heading: A test for right angles
paragraphs.text: One handy consequence is a quick check for perpendicular vectors. The cosine of a right angle is zero, so two vectors at 90 degrees have a dot product of zero. In fact, two non-zero vectors are orthogonal, meaning at right angles, exactly when their dot product is zero. At the other extreme, two vectors pointing the same way give the product of their lengths.

paragraphs.heading: Rules it follows
paragraphs.text: Scaling either vector by a number scales the answer by that number, and the dot product spreads over addition: 𝐚⋅(𝐛 + 𝐜) = 𝐚⋅𝐛 + 𝐚⋅𝐜. Together these make it what is called a bilinear form. A vector dotted with itself is never negative, and it is zero only for the zero vector. If vectors are written as columns, the dot product is also the matrix product of the transpose of 𝐚 with 𝐛.

paragraphs.heading: No cancelling allowed
paragraphs.text: With ordinary numbers, if ab = ac and a is not zero, then b must equal c. The dot product breaks this habit. Knowing 𝐚⋅𝐛 = 𝐚⋅𝐜 only tells you that 𝐚 is perpendicular to the difference 𝐛 − 𝐜. That difference can be a non-zero vector, so 𝐛 and 𝐜 may well be different.
